981: B is correct because the company already uses IAM Identity Center, so creating permission sets with granular permissions for Amazon RDS and Amazon S3 and assigning them to groups provides centralized, least-privilege access with minimal operational overhead. IAM Identity Center manages user credentials and access centrally, eliminating the need to create and maintain individual IAM users or per-team IAM role assignments. This native integration satisfies least privilege and confidentiality requirements with less administration than IAM users or a multi-account role topology.
982: B is correct because IAM Roles Anywhere enables workloads outside AWS, such as the on-premises virtual machines, to obtain temporary security credentials by exchanging X.509 certificates, so no long-term access keys are ever stored on the machines. The application assumes the role through the AWS CLI and receives only temporary access to the S3 bucket, which satisfies the requirement for secure, temporary access. Alternatives based on bucket IP policies or permanent IAM user access keys do not provide authenticated, short-lived credentials.
983: D is correct because AWS Transit Gateway acts as a central network hub that connects the VPCs of many accounts, and associating the Direct Connect connection with the transit gateway lets all new accounts reach the on-premises directory and DNS services over the existing DX link. This gives quick, consistent, and cost-effective access through a single shared connection. Creating separate DX connections or VPNs in every new account duplicates infrastructure and adds significant cost and management burden.
984: A is correct because Amazon CloudFront is a global CDN with hundreds of edge locations that cache content close to customers worldwide, improving latency and reducing load on the existing ALB and EC2 Auto Scaling group when serving millions of global customers. Using the current ALB as the origin requires no architectural change, and CloudFront's pay-as-you-go pricing makes it the cost-optimized choice for global delivery.
985: B is correct because Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent-access, infrequent-access, and archive tiers based on changing access patterns, which optimizes cost when some data goes unused for months while other data is used continuously. It maintains the same 11 nines of durability and high availability across multiple Availability Zones as S3 Standard. One Zone-IA sacrifices availability and durability, and Glacier Deep Archive is unsuitable for continuous access with business-hours peaks.
986: D is correct because Amazon EFS is a fully managed, highly available NFS file system that can be mounted concurrently by every EC2 instance in the Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones, providing shared access to the data with automatic capacity growth. Since the application reads shared file data, no significant code changes are needed, whereas EBS volumes can only be attached to one instance at a time and self-managed NFS or single-AZ file servers reduce resiliency and add management overhead.
987: A is correct because a Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and is purpose-built to handle TCP traffic with high throughput and connection handling, which matches the application's TCP-based communication at lower cost than an Application Load Balancer. B is correct because an Auto Scaling group automatically launches and terminates EC2 instances as user demand changes, delivering the required automatic scaling and high availability across the two Availability Zones. Together they provide the most cost-effective solution, whereas a Gateway Load Balancer is designed for virtual appliances and manual scaling cannot respond to demand.
988: A is correct because a tag policy in AWS Organizations defines the allowed values for the data-sensitivity tag key on EC2 instances and, with enforcement enabled, blocks tagging operations that use noncompliant values. D is correct because a service control policy can deny the RunInstances action when the required tag key is missing and deny actions that delete tags, ensuring IAM identities cannot launch untagged instances or remove existing tags. Attaching both policy types to the appropriate OU enforces tagging governance at the organization level.
989: C is correct because setting the RDS automated backup retention period to 30 days causes older automated backups to expire automatically, while manual snapshots never age out on their own and must therefore be manually deleted once they exceed 30 days. This uses native RDS features and satisfies the 30-day policy for both backup types at the lowest cost and effort. Introducing AWS Backup or CloudFormation automation adds unnecessary complexity and expense.
990: C is correct because Amazon EFS is a fully managed, highly available NFS file system that natively supports the NFS protocol, so the legacy application can migrate to AWS without any code or protocol changes. EBS provides block storage attachable to only a single instance, DataSync is a transfer service rather than a storage target, and EMRFS is specific to Amazon EMR clusters, so none fit the NFS requirement.
991: C is correct because Amazon SQS durably buffers the incoming tracker coordinates in a queue, decoupling the trackers from the EC2 web application so that unexpected spikes no longer overwhelm the instances or cause data loss. The application polls the queue and processes messages at its own pace, and any unprocessed messages remain in the queue for later replay. This requires minimal changes and delivers the least operational overhead compared to scanning S3 or DynamoDB or building Lambda-based ingestion.
992: B is correct because placing the RDS Multi-AZ cluster in private subnets keeps the database fully isolated from the public internet, and a Site-to-Site VPN between the office customer gateway and the VPC provides an encrypted private tunnel for the desktop client's direct connectivity to the cluster. This is the most secure option because public subnets expose the database to the internet, and security groups or office IP ranges alone do not provide private network connectivity from on premises.
993: C is correct because data transfer between EC2 instances within the same Availability Zone is free, whereas transfer between Availability Zones or Regions incurs per-GB charges. Placing all instances in the same AZ eliminates inter-instance data transfer costs for the batch processing workload, which directly reduces the overall data transfer costs.
994: A is correct because AWS Secrets Manager encrypts the database credentials with a KMS key and provides built-in automated rotation, and configuring a custom rotation period of 14 days directly satisfies the security guideline. Associating the secret with the Aurora DB cluster lets the application retrieve current credentials automatically, requiring the least operational effort. The alternatives all require building and maintaining custom Lambda rotation code with Parameter Store, EFS, or S3.
995: B is correct because Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate runs the video processing microservices in serverless containers that scale on demand, and Fargate's per-task pricing is cost-effective for spiky, long-running jobs like 20-minute video processing. Storing video content in S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically optimizes storage costs for terabyte-sized objects with varying access. Lambda is ruled out by its 15-minute execution limit, and the EKS option adds infrastructure management while Glacier Deep Archive is inappropriate for content being actively processed.
996: C is correct because AWS Fargate with Amazon EKS supplies compute capacity for Kubernetes pods without the company provisioning or managing any underlying EC2 nodes or control-plane infrastructure. A Fargate profile simply designates which pods run on Fargate, and AWS manages scaling, patching, and capacity. Self-managed nodes, managed node groups, and Karpenter all still require administering EC2 compute, so they carry greater operational overhead.
997: C is correct because Aurora Serverless automatically and instantly scales database capacity up and down with application traffic and only charges for the capacity actually consumed, making it the most cost-effective choice for variable workloads. Aurora provides a fully managed, structured relational database for user profiles, settings, and transactional data, along with automated backups to S3. Self-managed databases on EC2 require the company to handle patching, backups, and capacity itself, and Aurora Serverless avoids the fixed cost of provisioned RDS instances.
998: A is correct because a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 provides private connectivity between the VPC and S3 entirely over the AWS internal network, and adding the endpoint route to the subnet route table ensures uploads bypass the public S3 endpoint. This requires no extra cost or infrastructure. S3 buckets cannot be moved into a VPC, access points do not change the network path, and Direct Connect is unnecessary for private S3 access.
999: B is correct because an ElastiCache for Redis cluster caches the frequently read, rarely updated product catalog data in memory, which drastically reduces the CPU load on the RDS DB instance during catalog searches. With lazy loading, the cache is populated on demand as items are requested, so the website retrieves catalog data from the cache instead of repeatedly querying MySQL. The other options either target the wrong tier or do not address the database CPU bottleneck.
1000: B is correct because a Volume Gateway with cached volumes stores the primary data in Amazon S3 while retaining only the most recently accessed data on premises, giving the applications low-latency access to frequently used data despite the on-premises storage limitation. The volumes appear as iSCSI block devices to the on-premises applications, so they can retrieve frequently accessed data with low latency and minimal integration effort. Stored volumes require the full data set to remain on premises, which the limited space cannot accommodate, and Tape and S3 File Gateways target backup archives and SMB file workloads rather than low-latency block access.
